thread.title: What's the Meta with This Settlement? - Commentary Magazine
thread.title_full: What's the Meta with This Settlement? - Commentary Magazine

author: Christine Rosen
title: What's the Meta with This Settlement? - Commentary Magazine
text:
Everyone loves seeing a Goliath brought low, which is why critics of the tech industry immediately celebrated the announcement in late August that Meta had agreed to settle a lawsuit filed by 52 state and local attorneys general accusing the company that owns Facebook and Instagram of knowingly making its products addictive and harmful to children.
The $17.1 billion settlement features significant concessions on the company’s part designed to rectify children’s experience on Meta’s platforms, most notably Instagram. Disturbing evidence gathered from whistleblowers exposed just how cynical the company’s glossy marketing campaigns had been: “At Meta, we’re consistently making changes to provide teens with safe, protected experiences, and bring parents more peace of mind,” the company claimed, while regularly underreporting or disregarding known harms to children on its platforms.
Meta agreed to changes such as enhanced age-verification technologies; a default two-hour limit on children’s use of the platform; banning the use of certain photo filters for kids; and a “school mode” that turns off notifications during the school day and mutes notifications after midnight, among other things. (Most of these tools can be disabled by parents, so they are effectively optional.) The settlement also requires that an independent auditor report on Meta’s compliance with the agreement, although there does not appear to be any significant way to penalize Meta if it does not. Meta also cannot continue making false statements about its safety features, as it has done for nearly two decades.
Still, this settlement is better understood as a small step in the right direction rather than a significant victory for people who would like to see a broader reckoning for social media companies.
First, Meta did not admit guilt or wrongdoing, and the settlement agreement cannot be used as evidence of either in future cases (such as the one filed by the State of Florida, which did not join the settlement). Second, although the settlement figure sounds large, and the state AGs who brought the case were eager to use words like “sweeping” and “historic” in touting their win, it does nothing to force Meta to alter its business model. The dollar amount is also a drop in the bucket compared with, say, the tobacco settlements of the 1990s, which obliged four companies to pay more than $200 billion.
One of the unique challenges of Meta (as well as other social media platforms) is that it does not produce a single product; rather, it profits by harvesting human attention, which it turns into data for which advertisers pay. In other words, Meta is not Big Tobacco, both because of its business model and also because of its ubiquity. If you want to make the comparison more apt, it is better to think of social media use not like cigarette smoking, as technology critic Jaron Lanier told the New York Times, but “as if someone had added nicotine to the water supply.” Meta is still in the water supply, and it will continue to profit from data extracted from users, including children.
In fact, the company arguably will have access to even more data if it institutes its new age-verification policies, which worries privacy advocates. Meta will have a freer hand to justify more intrusive surveillance of users, including device-tracking to prevent a child from opening multiple fake accounts to bypass time limits, for example.
Not to mention that a $17.1 billion settlement is hardly punitive for a company whose profits last quarter alone were $60.8 billion and whose current total valuation is $1.47 trillion. Mark Zuckerberg is comfortable making mistakes that cost him billions. His failed Metaverse experiment, for example, is estimated to have cost the company $70 billion. Given that the settlement also gives Meta 10 years to distribute the penalties, it is no wonder Meta’s stock rose after news of the settlement.
In the long term, this settlement will likely benefit the company because it might serve as a form of regulatory-capture-by-lawsuit. Meta can easily absorb the costs while forcing the hand of other companies to comply with changes it negotiated: $5 billion of the settlement money hinges on state AGs persuading TikTok, Snap, and YouTube to agree to the same terms as Meta. As the New York Times’ DealBook noted, Meta “was willing to absorb some financial punishment to handicap rivals.”
Finally, the settlement highlights a failure of our political system. These lawsuits and settlements are happening in part because Congress has failed to pass any meaningful legislation to protect children on social media. Meta is not even the platform on which most kids spend most of their time; that ignominious distinction is shared by TikTok and YouTube. If, as a society, we decide that social media platforms are as harmful to minors as alcohol or tobacco, then we should regulate and age-restrict them with the same vigor we apply when it comes to those vices. Yet efforts to offer legislative guidance, such as the Kids Online Safety Act, languish.
This settlement cannot resolve several crucial questions about technology use that continue to bedevil us: Do we believe social media is a harmful substance that should be regulated? If so, what might those regulations look like? As a practical matter, is it feasible for the burden of regulating technology use to be placed entirely on parents, as many conservative and libertarian observers claim it should be?
Here, the comparison to cigarettes is instructive. Imagine a world where a parent refuses to allow her teenager to smoke at home, but when the teenager goes to school, his teacher gives him a pack of cigarettes. Some kids might still refuse to smoke, guided by the values they learned at home, but many others would enthusiastically light up. This is effectively the approach to children’s technology exposure today, when students are issued Chromebooks or iPads in kindergarten, with safety features that are easily evaded. Daily life is now structured in a way that makes it difficult to navigate without smartphones and social media. Schools and local governments tend to post news first on social media; parent groups often communicate entirely through Meta’s Facebook or WhatsApp; and good luck finding a job if you don’t have a presence on LinkedIn.
There is no single settlement or law that can solve these challenges. Nevertheless, whatever the limitations of the Meta settlement, and the benefits that this backdoor form of regulatory capture might bring to the company, it should still be understood as a significant moment: The era of cultural capture by Big Tech companies like Meta might be coming to an end. For 20 years, social media companies promised to “make the world more open and connected” and to “capture and share the world’s moments,” as Facebook’s and Instagram’s slogans claimed. No one believes that anymore. The country’s collective hangover from social media’s impact on our relationships, our politics, and our civic culture is finally here.
Historically, Americans have been unusually enthusiastic about technological innovation. Decades of decline in trust in government and our institutions, plus the behavior of many Big Tech companies, have squandered some of that enthusiasm. The Meta settlement should be understood as part of that story, as well as an expression of concern about the likely impacts of many new technologies. This includes AI and the data centers required to power its use, along with the ubiquitous surveillance made possible by technologies like Flock cameras. Rejecting the self-serving narrative of inevitability peddled by many of the nation’s technocratic and political elite is a sign of healthy democratic skepticism, not ignorance, conspiratorial thinking, or Luddism.
It won’t be a single stone that fells any one of the tech giants, nor should it be the goal of the government or trial lawyers to seek their downfall. Rather, we should celebrate a cultural shift that encourages citizens to push back and demand accountability from the technology companies whose products are embedded deeply in their daily lives and, more important, from the political leaders whose job it is to represent the interests of their constituents and to legislate accordingly.
